hints: Notice the air column above the water gets longer as water runs out, and a louder sound means resonance of that air column.
Recall the water surface acts as a closed end with a displacement node while the open top has an antinode, giving resonances at $\lambda/4$, $3\lambda/4$, $5\lambda/4$ and so on.
Compare two successive louder sounds and work out how much extra length is added to the air column in terms of wavelength.
walkthrough: The tuning fork drives sound into the air column above the water. The top is open and the water surface is closed, so a stationary wave forms only for certain air-column lengths.
The resonance condition for a closed tube is $L = \lambda/4$, then $3\lambda/4$, then $5\lambda/4$, and so on, with a node at the water and an antinode near the open top.
A louder sound is heard each time resonance occurs, so moving from one louder sound to the next increases $L$ from one allowed value to the next.
The increase is therefore $3\lambda/4 - \lambda/4 = \lambda/2$, and similarly for later pairs.
Set this equal to the measured change: $\lambda/2 = 32 \text{ cm}$.
Hence $\lambda = 2 \times 32 \text{ cm} = 64 \text{ cm}$. This is option C.

options.A: Half of 32 cm would be the distance from a node to an antinode, not the distance between two successive resonances.
options.B: 32 cm is the increase in air-column length, which equals only half a wavelength for a tube closed at the water surface.
options.C: Successive resonances are $\lambda/2$ apart in air-column length, so $\lambda = 2 \times 32 \text{ cm} = 64 \text{ cm}$.
options.D: 128 cm is four times the measured 32 cm change and confuses the quarter-wavelength first resonance with the half-wavelength separation.
